title: Ἀστεροπαῖος
about: Achilles refuses Lycaon’s plea: ransom is over since Patroclus died, and he too, great as he is, must die some dawn or evening or noon. Lycaon’s knees give way, Achilles stabs him at the collar-bone, throws the body into the river and taunts it, saying the fish will eat Lycaon’s fat and the river will not save the Trojans. The river, enraged, puts strength into Asteropaeus, a Paeonian ally, grandson of the river Axius, who stands against Achilles with two spears and throws both at once: one is stopped by the gold of the shield, the other grazes Achilles’ forearm. Achilles’ spear sticks in the bank; Asteropaeus tries three times to pull it out, but Achilles cuts him down with the sword and boasts that Zeus’ offspring is mightier than any river’s, since even Oceanus fears Zeus’ thunder.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα μιν Πριάμοιο προσηύδα φαίδιμος υἱὸς
λισσόμενος ἐπέεσσιν, ἀμείλικτον δ’ ὄπ’ ἄκουσε·
sentences.l:
So then to him Priam’s glorious son spoke,
begging with words, but an unsoftened voice he heard;
sentences.i: So Priam’s glorious son spoke to him, begging with words, but the voice he heard was unyielding;
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph. ὣς ἄρα ‘so then’ closes Lycaon’s plea of the last part, and μιν is Achilles. Πριάμοιο … φαίδιμος υἱός ‘Priam’s glorious son’ is Lycaon, with φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ the stock epithet. προσηύδα is an imperfect, ‘was speaking to’, and λισσόμενος ‘begging’ is the present participle of λίσσομαι. ἐπέεσσιν is the dative plural of ἔπος, ‘with words’. ἀμείλικτον ‘unsoftened, unyielding’ (ἀ- and the root of μειλίσσω ‘soften’) agrees with ὄπ’, the elided ὄπα ‘voice’; the voice is Achilles’, and Lycaon hears it, ἄκουσε.

sentences.t: νήπιε μή μοι ἄποινα πιφαύσκεο μηδ’ ἀγόρευε·
sentences.l: “Foolish one, do not to me ransom make known, nor speak;
sentences.i: “Foolish one, do not talk to me of ransom, and do not speak of it;
sentences.n: Achilles answers. νήπιε is the vocative of νήπιος ‘foolish’, a rebuke here and not a gentle word. μοι is ‘to me’, and ἄποινα ‘ransom’ is a plural. πιφαύσκεο is a present imperative middle, ‘make known, tell of’, in the uncontracted epic ending -εο, so μή … πιφαύσκεο is ‘do not tell me of’; μηδ’ ἀγόρευε adds ‘nor speak’, with the same object understood. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
πρὶν μὲν γὰρ Πάτροκλον ἐπισπεῖν αἴσιμον ἦμαρ
τόφρά τί μοι πεφιδέσθαι ἐνὶ φρεσὶ φίλτερον ἦεν
Τρώων, καὶ πολλοὺς ζωοὺς ἕλον ἠδ’ ἐπέρασσα·
sentences.i: For before Patroclus met his fated day, it was dearer to me in my wits to spare some of the Trojans, and many I took alive and sold;
sentences.n: Achilles tells why he once took prisoners. πρὶν … ἐπισπεῖν ‘before … met’ takes the infinitive: ἐπισπεῖν is the aorist infinitive of ἐφέπω ‘come upon, meet’, and αἴσιμον ἦμαρ ‘fated day’ is the death that Patroclus met. τόφρα ‘until then, so long’ answers πρίν. The main clause has no subject: πεφιδέσθαι ‘to spare’, a reduplicated aorist infinitive of φείδομαι, is what ἦεν φίλτερον ‘was dearer’, and τί … Τρώων ‘some of the Trojans’ is its object, with the partitive genitive. φρεσί is ‘wits’. ἕλον ‘I took’ and ἐπέρασσα ‘I sold’ (the verb of 21.40) are aorists, and ζωούς ‘alive’ is what he took them as.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὅς τις θάνατον φύγῃ ὅν κε θεός γε
Ἰλίου προπάροιθεν ἐμῇς ἐν χερσὶ βάλῃσι
καὶ πάντων Τρώων, περὶ δ’ αὖ Πριάμοιό γε παίδων.
sentences.l:
but now there is not one who may escape death, whom a god, at least,
before Ilios into my hands may cast,
of all the Trojans, and above all of Priam’s sons.
sentences.i: But now there is no one who will escape death whom a god puts in my hands before Ilios, of all the Trojans, and above all of Priam’s sons.
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ‘but now’ sets the present against the past of the last unit. οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὅς τις … φύγῃ is ‘there is no one who may escape’: ἔσθ’ is ἔστι, ὅς τις ‘anyone who’ stands before θάνατον, the object of φύγῃ, and φύγῃ is an aorist subjunctive. ὅν κε … βάλῃσι is an aorist subjunctive with κε, ‘whom a god may cast’, and ἐν χερσὶ … ἐμῇς ‘into my hands’ says where; θεός γε ‘a god, at any rate’ names who does the casting. Ἰλίου προπάροιθεν is ‘before Ilios’. καὶ πάντων Τρώων is ‘of all the Trojans’, and περὶ δ’ αὖ … παίδων ‘and above all the sons’, where περί is an adverb ‘beyond’ and Πριάμοιο is the epic genitive in -οιο.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ φίλος θάνε καὶ σύ· τί ἦ ὀλοφύρεαι οὕτως;
sentences.l: But, friend, die you too; why do you grieve so?
sentences.i: But, friend, you too must die; why do you grieve like this?
sentences.n: φίλος is a vocative, ‘friend’, used harshly. θάνε is the aorist imperative of θνῄσκω, ‘die!’, and καὶ σύ is ‘you too’. τί ἦ is ‘why, then’, with ἦ the particle of surprise. ὀλοφύρεαι ‘you grieve’ is the present middle in the uncontracted -εαι, and οὕτως is ‘so, in this way’.

sentences.t: κάτθανε καὶ Πάτροκλος, ὅ περ σέο πολλὸν ἀμείνων.
sentences.l: Died also Patroclus, who was far better than you.
sentences.i: Patroclus too has died, who was far better than you.
sentences.n: κάτθανε is κατέθανε, an aorist of καταθνῄσκω ‘die’, with the augment dropped and κατά shortened to κάτ- before θ. ὅ περ … ἀμείνων is ‘who indeed (was) better’, and the verb ‘was’ is left out. σέο is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘than you’, after the comparative ἀμείνων ‘better’, and πολλόν ‘by much’ is an adverb.

sentences.t: οὐχ ὁράᾳς οἷος καὶ ἐγὼ καλός τε μέγας τε;
sentences.l: Do you not see what sort I too am, both fair and great?
sentences.i: Do you not see what a man I am, handsome and tall?
sentences.n: ὁράᾳς is the epic form of ὁρᾷς ‘you see’. οἷος is ‘of what sort’ in an indirect question, and καὶ ἐγώ is ‘I too’: Achilles compares himself with the dead Patroclus. καλός ‘fair, handsome’ and μέγας ‘great, tall’ are joined by τε … τε.

sentences.t: πατρὸς δ’ εἴμ’ ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μήτηρ·
sentences.l: And of a good father I am, and a goddess mother bore me;
sentences.i: I am the son of a good father, and a goddess was the mother who bore me;
sentences.n: πατρὸς … ἀγαθοῖο is a genitive of origin after εἴμ’ (elided εἰμί) ‘I am’, ‘I am of a good father’, with the epic genitive in -οιο. θεά ‘goddess’ stands beside μήτηρ ‘mother’, and γείνατο is the aorist middle of γείνομαι ‘bear’, said of the mother, Thetis, who is not named.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔπι τοι καὶ ἐμοὶ θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή·
sentences.l: but upon me too, you see, are death and strong fate;
sentences.i: but over me too, you see, hang death and a strong fate;
sentences.n: ἔπι is the accented ἐπί, standing for ἔπεστι ‘is upon’; its verb is shared by the two subjects, θάνατος ‘death’ and μοῖρα ‘fate’. τοι here is the particle ‘you see’ and not σοι ‘to you’, and καὶ ἐμοί is ‘to me also’. κραταιή ‘strong’ is the epic feminine of κραταιός. The same words, θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή, stand at 5.83, and the English is taken over from there.

sentences.t:
ἔσσεται ἢ ἠὼς ἢ δείλη ἢ μέσον ἦμαρ
ὁππότε τις καὶ ἐμεῖο Ἄρῃ ἐκ θυμὸν ἕληται
ἢ ὅ γε δουρὶ βαλὼν ἢ ἀπὸ νευρῆφιν ὀϊστῷ.
sentences.l:
there will be either a dawn or an evening or a midday
when someone shall take from me also my life, in war,
striking either with a spear or with an arrow from the bowstring.”
sentences.i: there will come a dawn or an evening or a midday when some man will take my life from me too in war, striking me either with a spear or with an arrow from the bowstring.”
sentences.n: The speech ends with the one certainty Achilles has. ἔσσεται ‘there will be’ is the future of εἰμί, and ἢ … ἢ … ἢ ‘either … or … or’ lists the three times of day; δείλη is the late part of the day, ‘afternoon, evening’. ὁππότε τις … ἕληται is ‘when someone shall take’, an aorist subjunctive middle; ἐκ … ἕληται is split (tmesis), ‘take out’, and θυμόν here is ‘life’. ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, and καί ‘also’ makes it ‘from me too’. Ἄρῃ is the dative of Ares, standing for ‘war’. ὅ γε ‘he’ is that same someone. βαλών ‘striking’ is an aorist participle; ἀπὸ νευρῆφιν ὀϊστῷ ‘with an arrow from the string’ has the suffix -φιν, which does the work of a preposition’s case ending.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοῦ δ’ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and then his knees were loosed, and his dear heart;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his knees gave way at once, and his heart too;
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph. τοῦ is Lycaon, ‘of him’, and αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot, then and there’. λύτο is a middle aorist of λύω, without the augment, and is passive in sense: the knees ‘were loosed’. γούνατα is the epic plural of γόνυ ‘knee’, and ἦτορ ‘heart’ is a neuter noun, the nominative joined to γούνατα. These words stand at Odyssey 24.345 for Laertes, and the English is taken over from there.

sentences.t:
ἔγχος μέν ῥ’ ἀφέηκεν, ὃ δ’ ἕζετο χεῖρε πετάσσας
ἀμφοτέρας·
sentences.l:
His spear indeed he let go, and he sat down, his hands outspread,
both;
sentences.i: He let go of the spear and sat down with both his hands outspread;
sentences.n: ἔγχος μέν ‘the spear, for its part’ is the object of ἀφέηκεν, an aorist of ἀφίημι ‘let go’ with the epic -εη-; it is presumably the spear of Achilles that Lycaon had held (21.71). ὃ δ’ ἕζετο is ‘and he sat down’, the same man, Lycaon, set against the spear he lets go. χεῖρε is the dual of χείρ ‘hand’, and πετάσσας is an aorist participle of πετάννυμι, ‘spreading out’; ἀμφοτέρας ‘both’ is feminine plural, agreeing with the dual in sense. The unit ends at the ano teleia after the first word of line 116.

sentences.t:
Ἀχιλεὺς δὲ ἐρυσσάμενος ξίφος ὀξὺ
τύψε κατὰ κληῗδα παρ’ αὐχένα, πᾶν δέ οἱ εἴσω
δῦ ξίφος ἄμφηκες·
sentences.i: but Achilles drew his sharp sword and struck him on the collar-bone beside the neck, and the whole double-edged sword sank into him;
sentences.n: The unit begins after the first word of line 116. ἐρυσσάμενος is an aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, and ξίφος ὀξύ is ‘sharp sword’. τύψε is an aorist of τύπτω ‘strike’; κατὰ κληῗδα is ‘at the collar-bone’, where κληΐς is the bone that closes the base of the neck, and παρ’ αὐχένα is ‘beside the neck’. The subject of δῦ, ‘sank’, is ξίφος ‘sword’, and πᾶν ‘the whole’ agrees with ξίφος, while εἴσω ‘inside’ and οἱ ‘in him’ say where it went. δῦ is the aorist ἔδυ without the augment, and ἄμφηκες ‘double-edged’ is the adjective of the sword. The unit ends after the third word of line 118.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρα πρηνὴς ἐπὶ γαίῃ
κεῖτο ταθείς, ἐκ δ’ αἷμα μέλαν ῥέε, δεῦε δὲ γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
and he, face down upon the earth,
lay stretched out, and out the dark blood flowed, and wet the earth.
sentences.i: and he lay stretched out face down on the earth, and the dark blood flowed out and soaked the earth.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 118. ὃ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and he’, Lycaon again. πρηνής ‘face down’ and ταθείς, the aorist passive participle of τείνω ‘stretched out’, say how he lay. ἐκ … ῥέε is split (tmesis), ‘flowed out’, an imperfect of ῥέω, and μέλαν ‘dark’ is the usual adjective of blood. δεῦε is an imperfect of δεύω ‘wet, soak’, with γαῖαν ‘earth’ as its object; the blood is its subject.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ Ἀχιλεὺς ποταμὸν δὲ λαβὼν ποδὸς ἧκε φέρεσθαι,
καί οἱ ἐπευχόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευεν·
sentences.l:
And him Achilles, to the river taking by the foot, sent to be carried off,
and over him, vaunting, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Achilles took him by the foot and sent him off into the river to be carried away, and, in triumph over him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: τόν is Lycaon, the object of ἧκε, an aorist of ἵημι ‘send, cast’. ποταμὸν δὲ is ‘to the river’, where the ending -δε is added to ποταμόν and gives the direction; the edition prints it as two words. λαβὼν ποδός ‘taking by the foot’ has a genitive for the part taken, and φέρεσθαι is a passive infinitive of purpose, ‘to be carried’. ἐπευχόμενος ‘vaunting over him’ is a present participle of ἐπεύχομαι, here a boast over a dead man. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ἀγόρευεν ‘he spoke winged words’ is the stock phrase, with the verb ἀγορεύω ‘speak’, as at 3.155; καί οἱ is ‘and to him’ (the dative governed by ἐπευχόμενος, ‘over him’).

sentences.t:
ἐνταυθοῖ νῦν κεῖσο μετ’ ἰχθύσιν, οἵ σ’ ὠτειλὴν
αἷμ’ ἀπολιχμήσονται ἀκηδέες·
sentences.l:
“Lie there now among the fishes, who your wound
the blood will lick away, uncaring;
sentences.i: “Lie there now among the fishes, who will lick the blood from your wound, uncaring;
sentences.n: Achilles’ taunt begins. ἐνταυθοῖ is an adverb, ‘here, in this place’, and κεῖσο is a present imperative middle of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. μετ’ ἰχθύσιν is ‘among the fishes’, a dative plural. ἀπολιχμήσονται is a future of ἀπολιχμάομαι ‘lick off’, with αἷμα ‘blood’ as the thing licked off and σ’ (σε) … ὠτειλήν ‘you, at the wound’ saying from whom and from where. ἀκηδέες is the plural of ἀκηδής, here active, ‘without care’, as the fish care nothing for the dead man; in the Odyssey the word is passive, ‘uncared for’ (20.130). The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 123.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σε μήτηρ
ἐνθεμένη λεχέεσσι γοήσεται, ἀλλὰ Σκάμανδρος
οἴσει δινήεις εἴσω ἁλὸς εὐρέα κόλπον·
sentences.i: and your mother will not lay you on a bed and lament you, but eddying Scamander will carry you into the broad bosom of the sea;
sentences.n: The unit begins after the third word of line 123. οὐδέ σε μήτηρ … γοήσεται is ‘nor will your mother lament you’, with γοήσεται the future of γοάω ‘wail for’. ἐνθεμένη is an aorist middle participle of ἐντίθημι ‘lay in’, ‘having laid you’; λεχέεσσι is the dative plural of λέχος ‘bed’, here the bier on which the dead are laid out for mourning. ἀλλὰ Σκάμανδρος οἴσει is ‘but Scamander will carry’, οἴσει the future of φέρω. Scamander is the river’s other name, Xanthus being the god’s name for it (20.74). δινήεις is ‘eddying’, the river’s epithet, as at 21.2. εἴσω ἁλὸς … κόλπον is ‘into the bosom of the sea’, and εὐρέα is the accusative of εὐρύς ‘broad’.

sentences.t:
θρῴσκων τις κατὰ κῦμα μέλαιναν φρῖχ’ ὑπαΐξει
ἰχθύς, ὅς κε φάγῃσι Λυκάονος ἀργέτα δημόν.
sentences.l:
leaping some fish along the wave, up through the dark ripple,
will dart, which shall eat Lycaon’s white fat.
sentences.i: and some fish, leaping, will dart up along the wave through the dark ripple and eat Lycaon’s white fat.
sentences.n: The subject is ἰχθύς ‘a fish’, which stands last in its clause, with τις ‘some’ earlier in the line. θρῴσκων is a present participle of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, and ὑπαΐξει is a future of ὑπαΐσσω ‘dart up from below’. κατὰ κῦμα is ‘along the wave’, and μέλαιναν φρῖχ’ ‘dark ripple’ is the accusative of φρίξ, the ruffled surface the fish breaks. ὅς κε φάγῃσι is a relative clause with an aorist subjunctive of ἐσθίω ‘eat’, ‘which shall eat’. Λυκάονος is Lycaon’s own name, Achilles naming his victim. ἀργέτα is an epic form meaning ‘white, bright’, agreeing with δημόν ‘fat’.

sentences.t:
φθείρεσθ’ εἰς ὅ κεν ἄστυ κιχείομεν Ἰλίου ἱρῆς
ὑμεῖς μὲν φεύγοντες, ἐγὼ δ’ ὄπιθεν κεραΐζων.
sentences.l:
Perish on, until we come to the town of sacred Ilium,
you fleeing, and I behind, ravaging.
sentences.i: Go on perishing, until we come to the town of sacred Ilium, you fleeing and I behind you, ravaging.
sentences.n: Achilles now speaks to the Trojans in general; ὑμεῖς ‘you’ is plural. φθείρεσθ’ is a present imperative middle of φθείρω, ‘perish, go to ruin’, said as a curse. εἰς ὅ κεν … κιχείομεν is ‘until we reach’: κιχείομεν is a first plural aorist subjunctive of κιχάνω with the epic short vowel, and κεν goes with εἰς ὅ. ἄστυ ‘town’ takes Ἰλίου ἱρῆς ‘of sacred Ilium’, where ἱρῆς is the Ionic form of ἱερῆς. ὑμεῖς μὲν φεύγοντες, ἐγὼ δ’ ὄπιθεν κεραΐζων sets the participles against each other; ὄπιθεν is ‘from behind’, and κεραΐζων ‘ravaging’ has no object stated.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὑμῖν ποταμός περ ἐΰρροος ἀργυροδίνης
ἀρκέσει, ᾧ δὴ δηθὰ πολέας ἱερεύετε ταύρους,
ζωοὺς δ’ ἐν δίνῃσι καθίετε μώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.l:
Nor will the river, though fair-flowing, silver-eddying,
help you, to which now for a long time many bulls you sacrifice,
and alive into its eddies you let down solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: Nor will the river help you, fair-flowing and silver-eddying though it is, the river to which you have long sacrificed many bulls and into whose eddies you let down solid-hoofed horses alive.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὑμῖν … ἀρκέσει is ‘nor will it help you’, with ἀρκέσει the future of ἀρκέω and ὑμῖν the dative ‘you’; the subject, ποταμός ‘river’, is the Scamander. περ ‘though’ goes with the adjectives, ἐΰρροος ‘fair-flowing’ and ἀργυροδίνης ‘silver-eddying’. ᾧ δή is ‘to which, as you know’, a relative with ποταμός as its antecedent. δηθά ‘for a long time’ and πολέας ‘many’ (epic for πολλούς) go with ἱερεύετε ‘you sacrifice’, with ταύρους ‘bulls’ as object. The horses are ζωούς ‘alive’, μώνυχας ‘solid-hoofed’, and καθίετε is ‘you let down’, a present of καθίημι; δίνῃσι is the epic dative plural of δίνη ‘eddy’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς ὀλέεσθε κακὸν μόρον, εἰς ὅ κε πάντες
τίσετε Πατρόκλοιο φόνον καὶ λοιγὸν Ἀχαιῶν,
οὓς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ θοῇσιν ἐπέφνετε νόσφιν ἐμεῖο.
sentences.l:
But even so you shall perish by an evil doom, until you all
pay for the slaughter of Patroclus and the ruin of the Achaeans,
whom by the swift ships you slew, apart from me.”
sentences.i: But even so you will perish by an evil doom, until you have all paid for the slaughter of Patroclus and the ruin of the Achaeans, whom you killed beside the swift ships when I was apart from them.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς is ‘but even so’. ὀλέεσθε is a future middle of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’, and κακὸν μόρον ‘an evil doom’ is the accusative of the doom they will die. εἰς ὅ κε … τίσετε ‘until you pay’ has τίσετε, an aorist subjunctive with the short vowel (the form is the same as the future) of τίνω ‘pay the price’; Πατρόκλοιο φόνον and λοιγὸν Ἀχαιῶν ‘the ruin of the Achaeans’ are what is paid for. οὓς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ θοῇσιν ἐπέφνετε is ‘whom beside the swift ships you slew’, with ἐπέφνετε a second plural aorist of φένω and νηυσί the epic dative plural of ναῦς; νόσφιν ἐμεῖο ‘apart from me’ has the genitive of separation, for Achilles was away from the ships.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, ποταμὸς δὲ χολώσατο κηρόθι μᾶλλον,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the river was enraged at heart the more,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the river was all the more enraged at heart,
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph. ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is ‘so he said’, and ποταμός is the river-god, named Xanthus at line 146. χολώσατο is an aorist middle of χολόω ‘enrage’, ‘became enraged’, and κηρόθι is ‘in the heart’; it is a locative of κῆρ ‘heart’, not the κήρ ‘death-spirit’. μᾶλλον ‘more’ says the river was angry already.

sentences.t:
ὅρμηνεν δ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ὅπως παύσειε πόνοιο
δῖον Ἀχιλλῆα, Τρώεσσι δὲ λοιγὸν ἀλάλκοι.
sentences.l:
and he pondered in his heart how he might stop
heavenly Achilles from his toil, and for the Trojans keep ruin away.
sentences.i: and he pondered in his heart how he might stop heavenly Achilles from his toil and keep ruin away from the Trojans.
sentences.n: ὅρμηνεν is a form of ὁρμαίνω ‘ponder’, the verb of a hero weighing a plan; ἀνὰ θυμόν is ‘in his heart’. ὅπως takes two optatives of purpose: παύσειε, from παύω ‘stop’, with πόνοιο ‘from his toil’ in the genitive, and ἀλάλκοι, from ἀλαλκεῖν ‘keep off, ward off’, with λοιγόν ‘ruin’ and Τρώεσσι ‘for the Trojans’ in the dative. δῖον Ἀχιλλῆα is ‘heavenly Achilles’, the object of παύσειε.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ Πηλέος υἱὸς ἔχων δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
Ἀστεροπαίῳ ἐπᾶλτο κατακτάμεναι μενεαίνων
υἱέϊ Πηλεγόνος·
sentences.i: Meanwhile the son of Peleus, holding his long-shadowed spear, leapt at Asteropaeus, the son of Pelegon, eager to kill him;
sentences.n: τόφρα δέ ‘meanwhile’ turns to the other action. Πηλέος υἱός is Achilles, and δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος is the stock ‘long-shadowed spear’. ἐπᾶλτο is an aorist of ἐφάλλομαι ‘leap at’, without the augment, with Ἀστεροπαίῳ in the dative. κατακτάμεναι is an aorist infinitive of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, ‘to kill him’, and μενεαίνων ‘eager’ goes with it. υἱέϊ Πηλεγόνος is the epic dative of υἱός, ‘to the son of Pelegon’, naming Asteropaeus’ father. The unit ends after the second word of line 141.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ Ἀξιὸς εὐρυρέεθρος
γείνατο καὶ Περίβοια Ἀκεσσαμενοῖο θυγατρῶν
πρεσβυτάτη· τῇ γάρ ῥα μίγη ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης.
sentences.l:
him Axius of the wide stream
begot, and Periboea, of Acessamenus’ daughters
the eldest; for with her was mingled the river, deep-eddying.
sentences.i: Axius of the wide stream was his father, and Periboea, the eldest of the daughters of Acessamenus, his mother; for the deep-eddying river had lain with her.
sentences.n: The unit begins after the second word of line 141. τὸν δ’ ‘and him’ is Asteropaeus. Ἀξιὸς is the river Axius of Paeonia, and εὐρυρέεθρος ‘of the wide stream’ is his epithet, a different word from εὐρὺ ῥέοντος ‘wide-flowing’ at line 157. γείνατο is singular with two subjects: Axius as father and Περίβοια as mother. Ἀκεσσαμενοῖο θυγατρῶν is ‘of the daughters of Acessamenus’, and πρεσβυτάτη is the superlative ‘eldest’. τῇ γάρ ῥα μίγη ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης is ‘for with her had lain the deep-eddying river’; μίγη is a passive aorist of μίγνυμι ‘mingle’ with a dative, said of a union. The river is Axius again.

sentences.t:
τῷ ῥ’ Ἀχιλεὺς ἐπόρουσεν, ὃ δ’ ἀντίος ἐκ ποταμοῖο
ἔστη ἔχων δύο δοῦρε·
sentences.l:
At him Achilles rushed, and he, opposite, out of the river
stood, holding two spears;
sentences.i: Achilles rushed at him, and Asteropaeus took his stand out of the river, facing him, holding two spears;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘at him’, Asteropaeus, and ἐπόρουσεν is an aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush at’. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ marks the other man, and ἀντίος ‘facing’ is the adjective of a man standing against another. ἐκ ποταμοῖο ἔστη is ‘stood out of the river’, either coming out of it or standing up from it; the Greek does not say which. ἔχων δύο δοῦρε ‘holding two spears’ has δοῦρε, the dual of δόρυ, and prepares the double throw of line 162. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 145.

sentences.t:
μένος δέ οἱ ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκε
Ξάνθος, ἐπεὶ κεχόλωτο δαϊκταμένων αἰζηῶν,
τοὺς Ἀχιλεὺς ἐδάϊζε κατὰ ῥόον οὐδ’ ἐλέαιρεν.
sentences.l:
and might in his wits put
Xanthus, for he was enraged for the young men cut down,
whom Achilles was cutting down along the stream and did not pity.
sentences.i: and Xanthus put might in his wits, for he was enraged at the young men who had been cut down, whom Achilles was cutting down along the stream and did not pity.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 145. μένος … θῆκε is ‘put might’, an aorist of τίθημι, with οἱ ‘in him’ (Asteropaeus) and ἐν φρεσί ‘in his wits’. Ξάνθος is the river’s name among the gods, here simply the river. κεχόλωτο is a pluperfect middle of χολόω ‘enrage’, ‘had been, was enraged’, and δαϊκταμένων αἰζηῶν is a genitive of cause, ‘because of the young men cut down’. αἰζηός is a vigorous young man, and δαϊκταμένων a participle built on the root of δαΐζω ‘cut down’; ἐδάϊζε is its imperfect. κατὰ ῥόον is ‘along the stream’, and οὐδ’ ἐλέαιρεν ‘did not pity’ is an imperfect.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l:
And when they were near, going against one another,
him first addressed swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, swift-footed, heavenly Achilles spoke to him first:
sentences.n: These two lines stand together, word for word, at 20.176–177, where Achilles meets Aeneas, and the English is taken over from there. οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν is ‘and when they were near’, with ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες ‘going against one another’. τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε is ‘first addressed him’, προσέειπε an aorist of προσεῖπον, and ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’. The speech that follows is Achilles’ question.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἰς ἀνδρῶν ὅ μευ ἔτλης ἀντίος ἐλθεῖν;
sentences.l: “Who among men are you, and from where, who dared to come opposite me?
sentences.i: “Who among men are you, and where from, you who dared to come against me?
sentences.n: Achilles asks his opponent his name and country, as a warrior does before a duel. τίς πόθεν εἰς ἀνδρῶν is ‘who, from where, are you of men’: εἰς is the epic form of εἶ ‘you are’, and ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ is partitive. ὅ μευ ἔτλης ἀντίος ἐλθεῖν is ‘who dared to come against me’; μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, and ἔτλης is the aorist of τλάω ‘dare’. ἀντίος ἐλθεῖν takes the genitive, ‘to come face to face with’.

sentences.t: δυστήνων δέ τε παῖδες ἐμῷ μένει ἀντιόωσι.
sentences.l: and of wretched men the sons meet my might.”
sentences.i: Only the sons of wretched men meet my might.”
sentences.n: δέ τε is ‘and’ with τε marking a general truth. δυστήνων … παῖδες is ‘the sons of wretched men’, and ἀντιόωσι is the third plural present of ἀντιάω ‘meet’ in its epic form with -όω-. ἐμῷ μένει is ‘my might’, a dative after ἀντιόωσι. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Πηλεγόνος προσεφώνεε φαίδιμος υἱός·
sentences.l: And him in turn addressed Pelegon’s glorious son:
sentences.i: Then Pelegon’s glorious son spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph. τὸν δ’ αὖ ‘and him in turn’ marks a reply, and Πηλεγόνος … φαίδιμος υἱός ‘Pelegon’s glorious son’ is Asteropaeus, called so as Lycaon was ‘Priam’s glorious son’ in line 97. προσεφώνεε is an imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘address’, and Πηλεγόνος is the genitive of Πηλεγών.

sentences.t: Πηλεΐδη μεγάθυμε τί ἦ γενεὴν ἐρεείνεις;
sentences.l: “Peleus’-son, great-hearted, why do you ask about my lineage?
sentences.i: “Great-hearted son of Peleus, why do you ask about my lineage?
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδη is the vocative of Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’, and μεγάθυμε is the vocative of μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’. τί ἦ is ‘why, then’. γενεήν is ‘birth, lineage’, and ἐρεείνεις is a present of ἐρεείνω ‘ask about, enquire after’. He answers Achilles’ question of line 150.

sentences.t:
εἴμ’ ἐκ Παιονίης ἐριβώλου τηλόθ’ ἐούσης
Παίονας ἄνδρας ἄγων δολιχεγχέας· ἥδε δέ μοι νῦν
ἠὼς ἑνδεκάτη ὅτε Ἴλιον εἰλήλουθα.
sentences.l:
I am from Paeonia, rich-soiled, being far away,
leading Paeonian men, long-speared; and this now for me
is the eleventh dawn since to Ilios I have come.
sentences.i: I am from Paeonia of the rich soil, far away, leading Paeonian men with long spears; and this is now the eleventh dawn for me since I came to Ilios.
sentences.n: εἴμ’ is εἰμί ‘I am’, with its last vowel elided. ἐκ Παιονίης ἐριβώλου is ‘from rich-soiled Paeonia’, with τηλόθ’ ἐούσης ‘being far off’ added in the genitive (ἐούσης is the epic form of οὔσης). ἄγων is ‘leading’, and δολιχεγχέας ‘long-speared’ is an accusative plural, from δολιχός ‘long’ and ἔγχος ‘spear’. ἥδε … ἠὼς ἑνδεκάτη is ‘this eleventh dawn’, the eleventh day counted from his arrival, and εἰλήλουθα is the perfect of ἔρχομαι ‘have come’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ γενεὴ ἐξ Ἀξιοῦ εὐρὺ ῥέοντος
Ἀξιοῦ, ὃς κάλλιστον ὕδωρ ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἵησιν,
sentences.l:
But my lineage is from Axius, wide-flowing,
Axius, who the fairest water over the earth sends,
sentences.i: But my lineage comes from Axius, the wide-flowing, Axius, who sends the fairest water over the earth,
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns to his descent. γενεή is ‘lineage’ again, with ἐξ Ἀξιοῦ ‘from Axius’; Axius is a river-god and the river in Paeonia, as in the Catalogue (2.849), and εὐρὺ ῥέοντος ‘wide-flowing’ is his epithet. The relative ὅς … ἵησιν is ‘who sends’, a present of ἵημι; κάλλιστον ὕδωρ is ‘fairest water’, a superlative, and ἐπὶ γαῖαν ‘over the earth’. The second Ἀξιοῦ, a genitive in apposition, repeats the name at the head of the relative clause.

sentences.t:
ὃς τέκε Πηλεγόνα κλυτὸν ἔγχεϊ· τὸν δ’ ἐμέ φασι
γείνασθαι·
sentences.l:
who begot Pelegon, famous with the spear; and him me, they say,
to have begotten;
sentences.i: who begot Pelegon, famous for his spear; and Pelegon, they say, begot me;
sentences.n: ὃς τέκε is ‘who begot’, an aorist of τίκτω, with Axius as the subject. Πηλεγόνα κλυτὸν ἔγχεϊ is ‘Pelegon, famous with the spear’, where ἔγχεϊ is a dative of respect. τὸν δ’ ἐμέ φασι γείνασθαι is ‘and they say that he begot me’: φασι ‘they say’ governs an infinitive, γείνασθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of γείνομαι, and the accusatives τόν (Pelegon, the subject) and ἐμέ (the object). The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 160.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖτε μαχώμεθα φαίδιμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ.
sentences.l: now then let us fight, glorious Achilles.”
sentences.i: Now let us fight, glorious Achilles.”
sentences.n: The unit begins after the first word of line 160. νῦν αὖτε is ‘now then’, αὖτε being a form of αὖτις ‘again, in turn’, here marking the move from words to fighting. μαχώμεθα is a first plural present subjunctive in the sense of an exhortation, ‘let us fight’. φαίδιμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ is the vocative, with φαίδιμε elided. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’ ἀπειλήσας, ὃ δ’ ἀνέσχετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
Πηλιάδα μελίην·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, threatening, and he held up, heavenly Achilles,
the Pelian ash-spear;
sentences.i: So he spoke in threat, and heavenly Achilles held up the Pelian ash-spear;
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph. ὣς φάτ’ is ‘so he spoke’, with φάτ’ the elided φάτο (ἔφατο without the augment), and ἀπειλήσας is an aorist participle of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’: Asteropaeus’ last words are a challenge. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Achilles, as the following δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς shows. ἀνέσχετο is an aorist middle of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’. Πηλιάδα μελίην is ‘the Pelian ash-spear’, the spear Chiron gave Peleus from Mount Pelion. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 162.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἁμαρτῇ δούρασιν ἀμφὶς
ἥρως Ἀστεροπαῖος, ἐπεὶ περιδέξιος ἦεν.
sentences.l:
and he, together, on both sides, with spears,
the hero Asteropaeus, for he was skilled with both hands.
sentences.i: and the hero Asteropaeus, who was skilled with either hand, threw with both his spears at once.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 162. The sentence has no verb of its own; the sense is that he threw, and the next lines say with what result. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, now Asteropaeus, named in line 163. ἁμαρτῇ ‘together, at the same time’ and δούρασιν ἀμφίς ‘with spears on both sides’ together mean he cast both spears at once, so the English supplies ‘threw’. ἥρως is ‘hero’. περιδέξιος is ‘skilled with both hands’, a compound of περί and δεξιός ‘right-handed’, and ἦεν is the epic form of ἦν. The reason is given by ἐπεί ‘since’.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ἑτέρῳ μὲν δουρὶ σάκος βάλεν, οὐδὲ διὰ πρὸ
ῥῆξε σάκος·
sentences.l:
and with the one spear he struck the shield, but not through
and out did he break the shield;
sentences.i: and with the one spear he struck the shield, but he did not break clean through it;
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ ‘and’ introduces the result of the throw. ἑτέρῳ μὲν δουρί is ‘with the one spear’, answered by τῷ δ’ ἑτέρῳ in line 166. σάκος βάλεν is ‘struck the shield’, the shield being Achilles’; βάλεν is the aorist ἔβαλεν without the augment. οὐδὲ διὰ πρό … ῥῆξε is ‘did not break through and out’: διά and πρό are adverbs, ‘through’ and ‘forward’, and ῥῆξε is an aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. The unit ends at the ano teleia after σάκος in line 165.

sentences.t: χρυσὸς γὰρ ἐρύκακε δῶρα θεοῖο·
sentences.l: for gold held it back, gifts of the god;
sentences.i: for the gold held it back, the gifts of the god;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 165. χρυσός ‘gold’ is the subject of ἐρύκακε, a reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’. δῶρα θεοῖο is ‘the gifts of the god’, in apposition to the gold; the god is Hephaestus, who made the shield (book 18), and θεοῖο is the epic genitive in -οιο. These words stand at 20.268, and the English is taken over from there. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἑτέρῳ μιν πῆχυν ἐπιγράβδην βάλε χειρὸς
δεξιτερῆς, σύτο δ’ αἷμα κελαινεφές·
sentences.l:
and with the other, him on the forearm, grazing, he struck of the hand,
the right, and the blood spurted, dark-clouded;
sentences.i: and with the other he struck him grazing, on the forearm of his right hand, and the blood spurted out, dark as a cloud;
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἑτέρῳ ‘and with the other’ completes the pair begun at line 164. μιν is Achilles, the accusative of the person, with πῆχυν ‘forearm’ the accusative of the part struck and χειρὸς δεξιτερῆς ‘of his right hand’ its genitive; δεξιτερῆς is an epic form of δεξιᾶς. ἐπιγράβδην ‘grazing’ is an adverb meaning scratching the surface. σύτο is a middle aorist of σεύω ‘rush’, here ‘spurted’, and κελαινεφές ‘dark as a cloud’ agrees with αἷμα ‘blood’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 167.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ
γαίῃ ἐνεστήρικτο λιλαιομένη χροὸς ἆσαι.
sentences.l:
and it, above him,
in the earth was fixed, longing to glut itself on his flesh.
sentences.i: and the spear flew past above him and stuck fast in the earth, longing to glut itself on his flesh.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 167. ἣ is feminine, ‘it’; the noun it takes up is the second spear, as ἐγχείη ‘spear’ is feminine. ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ is ‘above him’, over Achilles, and γαίῃ ἐνεστήρικτο is ‘was fixed in the earth’, a pluperfect passive of ἐνστηρίζω. λιλαιομένη ‘longing’ and ἆσαι, an aorist infinitive of ἄω ‘glut, sate’, give the spear a longing for χροός ‘flesh’ (a genitive). The picture is the same as at 21.69–70, where Achilles’ spear flew over Lycaon’s back.

sentences.t:
δεύτερος αὖτ’ Ἀχιλεὺς μελίην ἰθυπτίωνα
Ἀστεροπαίῳ ἐφῆκε κατακτάμεναι μενεαίνων.
sentences.l:
Second in turn Achilles his ash-spear, flying straight,
at Asteropaeus let fly, eager to kill him.
sentences.i: Next Achilles in his turn let fly his straight-flying ash-spear at Asteropaeus, eager to kill him.
sentences.n: δεύτερος αὖτ’ is ‘second, in turn’: after Asteropaeus’ double cast it is Achilles’ throw. μελίην is ‘ash-spear’ (the accusative of μελίη). ἰθυπτίωνα is a rare adjective, taken to mean ‘flying straight’, from ἰθύς ‘straight’ and the root of ‘fly’; this sense is the usual explanation and is not certain. ἐφῆκε is an aorist of ἐφίημι ‘let fly at’, with Ἀστεροπαίῳ in the dative. κατακτάμεναι μενεαίνων ‘eager to kill’ repeats line 140.

sentences.t:
καὶ τοῦ μέν ῥ’ ἀφάμαρτεν, ὃ δ’ ὑψηλὴν βάλεν ὄχθην,
μεσσοπαγὲς δ’ ἄρ’ ἔθηκε κατ’ ὄχθης μείλινον ἔγχος.
sentences.l:
And him he missed, and the high bank he struck,
and fixed it to its middle down into the bank, the ashen spear.
sentences.i: He missed him, but struck the high bank, and the ashen spear stuck in the bank up to its middle.
sentences.n: καὶ τοῦ μέν ῥ’ ἀφάμαρτεν is ‘and him he missed’; ἀφάμαρτεν is an aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω with a genitive, τοῦ, the object missed. ὃ δ’ ‘but he’ is Achilles still, and ὑψηλὴν … ὄχθην ‘the high bank’ is what he hit. μεσσοπαγές is a compound of μέσσος ‘middle’ and the root of πήγνυμι ‘fix’, so ‘fixed in the middle’; with ἔθηκε ‘made’ it is ‘made it stick up to the middle’, and κατ’ ὄχθης is ‘down into the bank’. μείλινον ἔγχος is ‘the ashen spear’.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ ἄορ ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
ἆλτ’ ἐπί οἱ μεμαώς·
sentences.l:
And Peleus’-son, his sharp sword drawing from beside his thigh,
leapt at him, eager;
sentences.i: and the son of Peleus drew his sharp sword from his thigh and leapt at him, eager;
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης is Achilles. ἄορ ὀξύ is ‘sharp sword’, ἄορ being the second of the poet’s words for it, with ξίφος, and ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle ‘drawing’. παρὰ μηροῦ is ‘from beside the thigh’, where the sword hung, the genitive of separation. ἆλτ’ is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’ with the augment dropped and the vowel elided; ἐπί οἱ is ‘at him’. μεμαώς ‘eager’ is the perfect participle. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 174.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρα μελίην Ἀχιλῆος
οὐ δύνατ’ ἐκ κρημνοῖο ἐρύσσαι χειρὶ παχείῃ.
sentences.l:
but he the ash-spear of Achilles
was not able to pull out of the steep bank with his stout hand.
sentences.i: while the other could not pull Achilles’ ash-spear out of the steep bank with his stout hand.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 174. ὃ δ’ ἄρα ‘but he’ is Asteropaeus, and μελίην Ἀχιλῆος is ‘the ash-spear of Achilles’, with Ἀχιλῆος the genitive of Ἀχιλλεύς. οὐ δύνατ’ is ‘was not able’, an imperfect of δύναμαι with the final vowel elided, and ἐρύσσαι is an aorist infinitive of ἐρύω ‘pull’. κρημνοῖο is a steep or overhanging bank, the same bank as ὄχθη in line 171, and χειρὶ παχείῃ ‘with his stout hand’ is a dative of means.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μέν μιν πελέμιξεν ἐρύσσασθαι μενεαίνων,
τρὶς δὲ μεθῆκε βίης·
sentences.l:
Three times he shook it, eager to pull it out,
and three times he let go of his strength;
sentences.i: Three times he shook it, eager to pull it out, and three times he eased off his strength;
sentences.n: τρίς ‘three times’ answers τρὶς δέ in the next line. μιν is the spear, and πελέμιξεν is an aorist of πελεμίζω ‘shake’. ἐρύσσασθαι is an aorist middle infinitive of ἐρύω, ‘to pull it out’, with μενεαίνων ‘eager’. μεθῆκε is an aorist of μεθίημι ‘let go, relax’, and βίης is a genitive after it, ‘he let up from his strength’, as one lets go of a strain. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 177.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ τέτρατον ἤθελε θυμῷ
ἆξαι ἐπιγνάμψας δόρυ μείλινον Αἰακίδαο,
sentences.l:
but the fourth time he wished in his heart
to break, bending back the ashen spear of the descendant of Aeacus,
sentences.i: but the fourth time he wanted in his heart to bend the ashen spear of Achilles back and break it,
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 177. τὸ δὲ τέτρατον is ‘the fourth time’, a neuter adverb. ἤθελε θυμῷ is ‘he wished in his heart’, and ἆξαι is an aorist infinitive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’. ἐπιγνάμψας is an aorist participle of ἐπιγνάμπτω ‘bend back’, with δόρυ μείλινον ‘the ashen spear’ as object. Αἰακίδαο is the epic genitive of Αἰακίδης, ‘the descendant of Aeacus’, who here is Achilles, Aeacus’ grandson. The sentence goes on into the next unit.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ πρὶν Ἀχιλεὺς σχεδὸν ἄορι θυμὸν ἀπηύρα.
sentences.l: but before that Achilles, near at hand, with his sword took away his life.
sentences.i: but before that, Achilles came near and took his life with the sword.
sentences.n: ἀλλά marks the break in what Asteropaeus tried. πρίν here is the adverb ‘before that’, and σχεδόν ‘near’. ἄορι is the dative ‘with the sword’, and ἀπηύρα is a past tense of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’, and its object is θυμόν, ‘took away his life’. This ends the sentence that began at line 177.

sentences.t:
γαστέρα γάρ μιν τύψε παρ’ ὀμφαλόν, ἐκ δ’ ἄρα πᾶσαι
χύντο χαμαὶ χολάδες·
sentences.l:
For in the belly he struck him beside the navel, and out all
poured to the ground his bowels;
sentences.i: For he struck him in the belly beside the navel, and all his bowels poured out on the ground;
sentences.n: γαστέρα … μιν τύψε is ‘struck him in the belly’, with μιν the person and γαστέρα the part struck; γάρ shows this explains the last unit. παρ’ ὀμφαλόν is ‘beside the navel’. ἐκ … χύντο is split (tmesis), ‘poured out’: χύντο is the aorist middle of χέω without the augment, with πᾶσαι … χολάδες ‘all the bowels’ as its subject. The unit ends after the third word of line 181, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν
ἀσθμαίνοντ’·
sentences.l:
and darkness covered his two eyes,
panting;
sentences.i: and darkness covered his eyes as he panted;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 181. τὸν δέ is ‘and him’, and ὄσσε is the dual ‘eyes’, so the pair is ‘him, the eyes’, the whole and the part. σκότος is ‘darkness’, which comes over the eyes of the dying, and κάλυψεν is an aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’. ἀσθμαίνοντ’ is the present participle of ἀσθμαίνω ‘pant’, agreeing with τόν. The unit ends at the ano teleia after the first word of line 182.

sentences.t:
Ἀχιλεὺς δ’ ἄρ’ ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὀρούσας
τεύχεά τ’ ἐξενάριξε καὶ εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.l:
and Achilles, upon his chest springing,
despoiled the armour, and, declaring, spoke a word:
sentences.i: and Achilles sprang on his chest, stripped off his armour and said, declaring aloud:
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 182. ὀρούσας is an aorist participle of ὀρούω ‘spring, rush’, and ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν is ‘on his chest’, in the epic dative plural. τεύχεά τ’ ἐξενάριξε is ‘and stripped off the armour’; the verb is an aorist of ἐξεναρίζω, ‘strip a slain man’, and τεύχεα is the uncontracted plural. εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα is ‘declaring, spoke a word’. Line 183 stands word for word at 13.618, and its English is taken over from there; the half-line before it is new here, and the English is fitted to it.

sentences.t:
κεῖσ’ οὕτως· χαλεπόν τοι ἐρισθενέος Κρονίωνος
παισὶν ἐριζέμεναι ποταμοῖό περ ἐκγεγαῶτι.
sentences.l:
“Lie there so; hard it is for you with the children of the son of Cronus, great in strength,
to quarrel, though sprung from a river.
sentences.i: “Lie there just as you are. It is hard for you, though sprung from a river, to quarrel with the children of the son of Cronus, great in strength.
sentences.n: κεῖσ’ is the imperative κεῖσο ‘lie’, elided, and οὕτως ‘so, just as you are’. χαλεπόν (ἐστι) τοι … ἐριζέμεναι is ‘it is hard for you to strive’; τοι here is σοι ‘for you’, and it is the word that the participle ἐκγεγαῶτι agrees with, a perfect participle of ἐκγίγνομαι ‘be born of’ with ποταμοῖο ‘from a river’ and περ ‘although’. ἐριζέμεναι is an epic infinitive of ἐρίζω ‘quarrel’ with the dative παισίν ‘the children’. ἐρισθενέος Κρονίωνος is ‘of the son of Cronus, great in strength’, Zeus.

sentences.t:
φῆσθα σὺ μὲν ποταμοῦ γένος ἔμμεναι εὐρὺ ῥέοντος,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ γενεὴν μεγάλου Διὸς εὔχομαι εἶναι.
sentences.l:
You say you are of the river’s race, flowing wide,
but I claim my lineage to be from great Zeus.
sentences.i: You say that you are of the race of the wide-flowing river, but I claim that my lineage is from great Zeus.
sentences.n: φῆσθα is the second singular of φημί ‘say’, in the epic form, and ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί ‘to be’. γένος is ‘race’ and εὐρὺ ῥέοντος ‘wide-flowing’ the river’s epithet, as at line 157; the river is Axius. σύ and ἐγώ are set against each other (μέν … αὐτάρ). γενεήν … εὔχομαι εἶναι is ‘I claim to be of the lineage’, with εὔχομαι ‘claim’ and an accusative of relation; μεγάλου Διός is ‘of great Zeus’.

sentences.t:
τίκτέ μ’ ἀνὴρ πολλοῖσιν ἀνάσσων Μυρμιδόνεσσι
Πηλεὺς Αἰακίδης· ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ Αἰακὸς ἐκ Διὸς ἦεν.
sentences.l:
A man begot me, being lord over many Myrmidons,
Peleus, descendant of Aeacus; and Aeacus was from Zeus.
sentences.i: My father is a man who is lord over many Myrmidons, Peleus, the descendant of Aeacus; and Aeacus was born of Zeus.
sentences.n: The edition prints τίκτέ with an acute on the final vowel as well; the word is τίκτε, an imperfect of τίκτω ‘beget’, and μ’ is με. ἀνὴρ … ἀνάσσων is ‘a man ruling’, with Μυρμιδόνεσσι the dative plural of the Myrmidons, Achilles’ people, and πολλοῖσιν ‘many’. Πηλεὺς Αἰακίδης names the father; Αἰακίδης means ‘descendant of Aeacus’ and here a son, since the next clause says Aeacus was himself ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’. ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ Αἰακός is ‘and Aeacus’, and ἦεν is the epic ἦν.

sentences.t:
τὼ κρείσσων μὲν Ζεὺς ποταμῶν ἁλιμυρηέντων,
κρείσσων αὖτε Διὸς γενεὴ ποταμοῖο τέτυκται.
sentences.l:
Therefore stronger is Zeus than the sea-flowing rivers,
and stronger in turn is the lineage of Zeus than a river’s.
sentences.i: So Zeus is stronger than the rivers that run to the sea, and the lineage of Zeus is stronger, in turn, than the lineage of a river.
sentences.n: τώ ‘therefore’ draws the conclusion. κρείσσων ‘stronger’ is a comparative with the genitive, ποταμῶν … ἁλιμυρηέντων ‘than the rivers’ and ποταμοῖο ‘than a river’ (with γενεή understood). ἁλιμυρηέντων is formed on ἅλς ‘salt, sea’ and a root meaning ‘flow’, so ‘sea-flowing’; the second half is not certain. αὖτε ‘in turn’ and τέτυκται, a perfect passive of τεύχω, ‘is made, is’, close the argument. Διὸς γενεή ‘the lineage of Zeus’ means Achilles himself.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ σοὶ ποταμός γε πάρα μέγας, εἰ δύναταί τι
χραισμεῖν·
sentences.l:
For you too, indeed, is a river at hand, a great one, if it can
help at all;
sentences.i: For you too have a great river beside you, if it can do anything to help;
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’, and σοί ‘for you’ is the dative of possession. πάρα is πάρεστι ‘is at hand’, and ποταμός … μέγας ‘a great river’ is the grandfather, Axius. εἰ δύναταί τι χραισμεῖν is ‘if it is able at all to help’, with χραισμεῖν the aorist infinitive of χραισμέω ‘help, avail’. The tone is sarcastic: Achilles doubts that it can. The unit ends at the ano teleia after χραισμεῖν.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔστι Διὶ Κρονίωνι μάχεσθαι,
τῷ οὐδὲ κρείων Ἀχελώϊος ἰσοφαρίζει,
οὐδὲ βαθυρρείταο μέγα σθένος Ὠκεανοῖο,
sentences.l:
but it is not possible to fight with Zeus, the son of Cronus,
with whom not even lord Achelous compares himself,
nor the great strength of deep-flowing Oceanus,
sentences.i: but one cannot fight against Zeus, son of Cronus, whom not even lord Achelous matches, nor the great strength of deep-flowing Oceanus,
sentences.n: The unit begins after the first word of line 193. οὐκ ἔστι … μάχεσθαι is ‘it is not (possible) to fight’, with Διὶ Κρονίωνι ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’ in the dative. τῷ is ‘with him’, and ἰσοφαρίζει ‘match himself with’ (from ἴσος ‘equal’) has two subjects, κρείων Ἀχελώϊος ‘lord Achelous’, a great river, and μέγα σθένος … Ὠκεανοῖο ‘the great strength of Oceanus’. βαθυρρείταο is the epic genitive of βαθυρρείτης ‘deep-flowing’, a variant of βαθύρροος. Ὠκεανός is the world-encircling river.

sentences.t:
ἐξ οὗ περ πάντες ποταμοὶ καὶ πᾶσα θάλασσα
καὶ πᾶσαι κρῆναι καὶ φρείατα μακρὰ νάουσιν·
sentences.l:
from whom all rivers and all the sea
and all springs and long wells flow;
sentences.i: from whom all rivers and all the sea and all springs and deep wells flow;
sentences.n: ἐξ οὗ περ is ‘from whom indeed’, and the relative is Oceanus. πάντες ποταμοί, πᾶσα θάλασσα, πᾶσαι κρῆναι and φρείατα μακρά all go with the single verb νάουσιν, the third plural of νάω ‘flow’. κρῆναι are springs, and φρείατα are wells, μακρά ‘long’ meaning that they are deep. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὃς δείδοικε Διὸς μεγάλοιο κεραυνὸν
δεινήν τε βροντήν, ὅτ’ ἀπ’ οὐρανόθεν σμαραγήσῃ.
sentences.l:
but even he fears the thunderbolt of great Zeus
and the dread thunder, when from heaven it resounds.”
sentences.i: but even he fears the thunderbolt of great Zeus and his dread thunder, when it resounds from heaven.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅς is ‘but even he’, Oceanus. δείδοικε is a perfect with present sense, ‘fears’, and its objects are Διὸς μεγάλοιο κεραυνόν ‘the thunderbolt of great Zeus’ and δεινὴν … βροντήν ‘dread thunder’. ὅτ’ ἀπ’ οὐρανόθεν σμαραγήσῃ is ‘when from heaven it resounds’: σμαραγήσῃ is an aorist subjunctive of σμαραγέω ‘resound, roar’, the suffix -θεν gives ‘from’, and the subject is not named, either Zeus or his thunder. The speech ends here.
